limitations: HRV data: sitting position of subjects may affect HRV, 2.5-minute epochs may not be sufficient to capture HRV, and noise in ECG records from wrist electrodes led to data exclusion (page 99-100).

Stressor: PASAT is an acute stressor and may not accurately characterize chronic stress regularly faced in office environments. Subjects tended to stop looking at their surroundings during the task, potentially weakening visual treatment effects (page 100-101).
Plant effect: The limited plant surface area in the study setup was not visually apparent enough to provide a stress reduction effect (page 101, 105).

Interpreting wood effect: It is unclear if the observed effects are a positive response to wood or a negative response to the non-wood (melamine foil) materials. Melamine may have negative connotations or elicit a negative reaction as a non-natural surface (page 101-102).
Attention measure: PASAT is not a conventional measure of attention for environmental psychology, and mathematical ability was a confounding factor (page 102).

Confounds: The experiment was single-blind, meaning the experimenter was aware of the study goals, potentially leading to unintentional non-verbal cues. Visible outside light reflecting between blinds was not controlled for, which could affect UV light exposure. A history confound is possible as all non-wood rooms were run first, though efforts were made to mitigate this (page 103-104).
Color: The study did not formally control for color, and the wood furniture was very light in color, raising concerns about whether the effect was due to wood or color (page 104).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the stress-reducing effects of wood and plants in an indoor office environment using a psychophysiological approach. Key findings indicate that wood visual surfaces significantly reduced sympathetic nervous system activation, as evidenced by lower skin conductance level (SCL) in the baseline period and lower frequency of non-specific skin conductance responses (F-NS-SCR) across all study periods. No significant effects were found for plants on sympathetic activation, nor for either wood or plants on parasympathetic activation (HRV) or attention (PASAT errors). Limitations include the acute nature of the stressor, potentially insufficient visual presence of plants, and methodological challenges with HRV measurement.
